read.text: This guide is for the facilitators of the IMNCI distance learning course. It follows the WHO IMCI distance learning facilitator guide (2014), in the wording of the Sudan national IMNCI protocol. The learners study the nine modules in this app; you hold three face-to-face meetings, follow their self-study, and assess them.

sections.title: The course and why distance learning
sections.goal: Explain what IMNCI is for, the objectives of the course, and its two core components.

read.text: Why IMNCI?

The IMNCI guidelines give simple, effective methods to manage the leading causes of serious illness and death in young children. Since IMCI was developed in the early 1990s, over 100 countries have adopted and adapted it, and thousands of health workers have been trained. Wide use has improved the quality of care and helped reduce child deaths.

cards.back: The health worker assesses all of the child's health: common illnesses, feeding and nutrition, immunization and other problems, not only the complaint the child is brought with.
IMNCI focuses on the most important causes of illness and death: acute respiratory infection, diarrhoea, malaria, measles, malnutrition and HIV.
It is for health centres, clinics and hospital outpatient departments. Doctors, nurses and other health workers who see sick children use it.
A sick young infant is up to 2 months. A sick child is 2 months up to 5 years: the child has not yet reached the fifth birthday.
Classifications decide whether a child is referred urgently, treated at the health facility, or managed safely at home.
Treatment follows the classification, not an exact diagnosis. It covers the most likely diseases behind each classification.

read.text:
IMNCI tells the health worker to:

  • check for signs of severe illness (general danger signs in the sick child, signs of very severe disease in the young infant)
  • assess the main symptoms, and the child's nutrition, immunization and feeding
  • classify each condition and identify its treatment, then decide on the treatment for all conditions
  • teach the caregiver how to care for the child at home, counsel to solve feeding problems, and say when to return
  • give follow-up care when the child comes back
Course objectives

At the end of the course, participants will be able to:

  • Use integrated case management for common health problems in sick young infants and children
  • Use the IMNCI chart booklet and recording forms in their clinical practice
  • Counsel caregivers on home treatment, feeding, care of the well child and disease prevention
Why distance learning?

A classroom IMNCI course needs health workers to travel and spend two weeks away from their work. That keeps many from being trained. Distance learning puts study into clinical practice: participants learn in their own time, at their own pace, and in their own health facility. It works only when participants also study with mentors and colleagues, and your role as facilitator is what makes them use the IMNCI tools in their own clinic.

steps.title: Face-to-face meetings
steps.text: You introduce new material, review the self-study periods and lead clinical practice. These meetings are the chance to clarify questions, solve problems, explain content and practise IMNCI together.

steps.title: Self-study periods
steps.text: Participants study the modules between meetings, practise IMNCI in their clinic and report back. They work with mentors, form study groups and seek support in their facility.

read.text: The self-study modules are the course "IMNCI distance learning modules" in this app. Each lesson opens only when the one before it is finished, and each module ends with a test. The app records what each learner has done, so you can follow progress between meetings.

sections.goal: Lay out the three meetings and two self-study periods, and fill in the course calendar.

read.text: The course runs for two to three months: three face-to-face meetings and two self-study periods.

steps.title: Meeting 1: Orientation (1 day)
steps.text: Introduce the IMNCI process, give out the learning materials and introduce Modules 1 and 2, explain the course structure and what is expected, and practise in the clinic as a group.

steps.title: Self-study period 1 (3 to 4 weeks): Modules 1 and 2
steps.text: Study the modules and their exercises, practise in the clinic and record cases on recording forms, complete the logbook exercises, meet the study group, keep in touch with mentors and facilitators.

steps.title: Meeting 2: Review and practice (1 day)
steps.text: Review progress and problems in self-study, look at cases from clinical practice, introduce the remaining modules, practise in the clinic.

steps.title: Self-study period 2 (6 to 8 weeks): the remaining modules
steps.text: The same activities as period 1, for Modules 3 to 9.

steps.title: Meeting 3: Final synthesis (1 day)
steps.text: Review progress and problems, look at cases, review all modules, practise in the clinic, the course assessment, and individual plans for continued learning.

read.text: If more modules are taught (for example HIV), more face-to-face meetings can be added. Each added meeting follows the agenda of Review and practice. Final synthesis is always the last meeting.

sections.title: The three face-to-face meetings
sections.goal: Say what each meeting is for and what participants must be able to do at its end.

read.text: You hold three meetings. In each you present IMNCI content and lead demonstrations and practice in a clinical setting. Your constructive feedback in these meetings is the heart of mentoring in a distance course.
Meeting 1: Orientation

• Explain the objectives and structure of the course, including the importance of clinical practice, mentors and study groups
  • Identify the main causes of child deaths
  • Explain the meaning and purpose of integrated case management, and describe the major steps of the IMNCI process
  • Show how the chart booklet and recording forms are job aids for the IMNCI process
  • Recognize the general danger signs in children
  • Identify important care for young infants, and explain why every young infant is assessed for very severe disease and feeding problems
  • Describe why a welcoming environment matters for case management, and show the key communication skills
  • Plan self-study, group study and clinical practice for Modules 1 and 2
Meeting 2: Review and practice

• Review self-study period 1, including cases from clinical practice, and address problem areas
  • Show the skills of Modules 1 and 2 in a clinical setting
  • Explain and show how to use the IMNCI charts to assess, classify and treat the main symptoms and conditions of a sick child
  • Plan self-study, group study, work with mentors and clinical practice for the remaining modules
Meeting 2 may be held at a health facility so that clinical skills can be practised on site.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: Meeting 3: Final synthesis

About three months after Meeting 1, the course closes. Participants review their self-study, you help with difficult areas, there is clinical practice, the assessment, and certificates. Participants learn about the follow-up after the course and may make an individual action plan.

• Review self-study period 2, including cases, and address problem areas
  • Explain and show the IMNCI clinical process with sick children and young infants
  • Use the IMNCI charts and recording forms well in clinical practice
  • Design an individual action plan for using IMNCI and improving their skills
What participants bring to every meeting

• ✔ Their modules, with any notes, exercises and review questions
  • ✔ Their logbook, with the written exercises and recording forms done
  • ✔ The IMNCI chart booklet

sections.title: Self-study modules and the logbook
sections.goal: Explain what the modules and the logbook hold, and how you use the logbook at each meeting.

read.text: The self-study modules hold the content of the course. Participants study in their own time and reinforce it through clinical practice, group study and mentors. Distance learning is flexible, but asks participants to manage their own time and study responsibly.
Each module has reading, video, and self-assessment exercises with their answers, so participants can check themselves. Participants should set a personal study calendar with goals for each module.
The course logbook

The logbook is where participants practise and record cases as they study. Review it at every meeting to see who is having difficulty, and deal with it with each participant. You also mark the logbook as one third of the course mark.

cards.back: After each module, about 20 multiple-choice and true/false questions on what was just studied. The answer key for each module is in this guide (Following each module). Use it to mark the exercises at the meetings.

As participants practise in the clinic they fill in IMNCI recording forms. You set how many per module or per period: at least 2 per module. They bring them to Meetings 2 and 3, where you review them for problem areas.
Participants tick the clinical signs they see during self-study. At the meetings, look for signs they are not seeing in their clinics, and arrange to show them in clinical practice or on video.

read.text: Each module in the app ends with its test ("Review questions and Module n test"). The app keeps each learner's result, so the logbook exercises can be checked before the meeting. Recording forms from the clinic are still kept on paper, or in the app's recording form.
read.label: In this app
Open a module test
read.text: The test at the end of each module is the logbook exercise for that module.

sections.title: Support during self-study
sections.goal: Set up the support each participant needs between meetings: study groups, mentors, the in-charge, and you.

read.text: Participants should involve others in their learning: people who explain the reading, help them see cases and signs, and help with difficulties. This support matters most in distance learning.

cards.back: Help participants form groups at the Orientation, by where they live and work. Groups meet regularly (weekly or twice a week) to review content, answer questions, explain confusing topics and practise skills together. Advice is in the Annexes.
Each participant names mentors they can go to: IMNCI-trained health workers or more experienced professionals, in their facility or outside it (for example at the district hospital).
The doctor or nurse in charge of the facility. Participants debrief them after each meeting. The in-charge should know the IMNCI guidelines and tools the participant will use in the clinic.
You may arrange practice at a nearby hospital. Give participants a letter certifying that they are in the course and that practice has been arranged with that facility.
Be clear about when participants should contact you (for example, a problem in clinical practice), and how and when you can be reached.

read.text: Using mobile phones

• Send a weekly SMS to remind participants where they should be in their reading and clinical practice.
  • Encourage participants to call or message you with questions. You can also call each week to check in.
Between meetings, the app shows course managers how far each learner has gone in the modules. Use it to see who is behind, and contact them.

sections.title: What is expected of participants
sections.goal: Tell participants what the course expects of them, what they receive, and how their feedback is gathered.

read.text: The course is for health workers who manage children at first-level facilities: nurses, nurse assistants and clinical health workers.
To complete the course, participants:

• ✔ Attend all face-to-face meetings
  • ✔ Read all self-study materials
  • ✔ Complete the exercises in the logbook
  • ✔ Practise IMNCI in their own facility
  • ✔ Use recording forms in clinical practice
  • ✔ Take an active part in the course
  • ✔ Learn with others as much as possible, and find mentors in their facility
  • ✔ Show professionalism and courtesy to facilitators, other participants and patients during clinical practice
  • ✔ Practise to the ethical and professional standards of the facilities

Before the course, participants and their in-charge officers should understand the commitment: one day away from the clinic for each meeting, plus time to study and practise. Ideally the in-charge encourages the participant.

Participants who meet all the course requirements receive a certificate of completion, certifying that they are trained in IMNCI through the distance learning course offered by the Ministry of Health and WHO.
Gathering feedback

steps.title: Meeting evaluations
steps.text: At the end of each meeting. They show gaps in the course and suggest changes. The forms are in the Annexes.

steps.title: Check-in forms
steps.text: At the start of Meetings 2 and 3: how the self-study period went, how long modules took, whether videos were used. Enter the answers in the course tracking sheet.

steps.title: Course evaluation
steps.text: Completed before certificates are given.

read.text: Feedback helps you serve the present participants, prepare future courses, and inform the planners at state and national level. Share good practices and problems with course logistics.
After the course

1. In the final meeting, participants may write an individual action plan: continued learning, using IMNCI in the clinic, working with mentors, sharing the tools in their facility.
  2. In the months after the course, participants are followed up for how they use IMNCI in practice.

sections.title: How participants are assessed
sections.goal: Mark the three parts of the course assessment and calculate the final mark.

read.text: The course mark has three parts of equal weight: each is about one third of the total.

cards.back: The module exercises and the recording forms from clinical practice. Marked for completion: up to 10 points per module, for how completely the exercises are answered and how many of the requested forms are handed in.

At Meeting 3, by the OSCE approach (objective structured clinical examination): either examination of real patients, or skills stations with video, photographs and case studies. Marked for accuracy: 1 point per correct answer.
About 30 multiple-choice questions on all modules, at Meeting 3. Marked for accuracy: 1 point per correct answer.

read.text: After the course

Follow-up visits in the participant's facility are strongly recommended, especially after a distance course: you see how well IMNCI is used in the clinic. WHO tools for this: the Health facility survey (2003) and Follow-up after training (1999).

sections.title: Preparing to be a facilitator
sections.goal: Describe who facilitates, how many are needed, and the three things a facilitator does.

read.text: Facilitators should already have completed the IMNCI case management course and the IMNCI facilitator course. A good facilitator is an experienced clinician who can teach, knows clinical practice and the national child health policies, is willing to lead discussion, and serves as a mentor as well as an instructor.
Your role is to help participants learn by giving encouragement, information and guidance, while prompting them to develop their own abilities.
read.label: Remember

read.text: Facilitating a distance course

This is a self-learning course, so promote self-learning. In the meetings, do not overload participants with too much in a short time: introduce the wider topics and skills, and prepare them to read in detail during self-study. Between meetings, make sure they get support and mentoring as they study and practise.

• Hold meetings in or near health facilities with a good caseload, to maximise clinical practice and avoid losing time moving between places.
  • Two facilitators for every 15 participants: for 25 to 30 participants, four facilitators.
  • Facilitators also attend a two-day training on facilitating the distance course, which is quite different from the classroom course.
What a facilitator does

cards.back: Explain content in full, with examples from clinical practice. Answer questions fully as they come. Give constructive feedback. Make sure participants know what is expected of each activity. Vary the way you teach: explain, show examples (video, photographs, cases), practise (role plays, demonstrations, clinical practice), reinforce (questions, discussion, feedback). Find gaps and give more explanation and practice. Model good clinical and communication skills.

Affirm correct answers, teamwork and progress. Bring the material alive with dynamic activities, and share clinical experiences. Encourage questions so nobody goes home confused. Remove obstacles to learning: noise, poor light, mobile phones. Make sure participants have support during self-study, and encourage ownership.

Plan each meeting ahead: notes, materials, the clinical practice sessions. Monitor each participant's progress by asking questions, reviewing their work and watching them practise. Give on-site mentoring, or help their mentors, during self-study.

read.text: Tips

Be available:

  • Show enthusiasm for the material and for the participants' learning.
  • Give the course your full attention: no unrelated work, phone or email in sessions or breaks. Breaks are time to mentor participants.
  • Be attentive to participants' needs, and encourage them to come to you with questions or feedback.

Create a good learning environment:

  • Build a friendly relationship by active listening and affirmations ("yes, I see what you mean", "that is a good question").
  • Watch participants as they work, and offer help to anyone not engaged.
  • Ask open questions: "What questions do we have about chest indrawing?" rather than "Does anyone have a question?"
  • Give enough time for answers. Be respectful, and never let anyone embarrass another participant.

Keep participants engaged:

  • Bring the content alive with your own experience. Do not read from the slides or your notes.
  • Let participants share experiences, questions and feedback: you should not lead the show.
  • Do not call on a named participant to answer in front of the group. If you want to check one person's understanding, do it individually.
  • Use this guide as your outline for materials, content and flow.

sections.title: Materials and preparing each meeting
sections.goal: Prepare the materials, the room and the equipment so each meeting runs to time.

read.text: The meetings are full of information and their flow is different from the classroom course. Prepare well so that everything is covered.
Materials for facilitators

• This facilitator guide.
  • The slides for each meeting: visuals and key points only, do not rely on them. Print them where power cuts are likely.
  • The course tracking sheet: participant list, check-in answers, marks, and the course budget.
  • The implementation guide for IMNCI distance learning, to check that all preparations are done.
  • The IMNCI training videos. They are older than the present chart booklet (for example for fever and malnutrition), so use them to show the process of an assessment.
  • The national IMNCI chart booklet and recording forms (sick child and young infant).
For each participant

• Notebook, pens and pencils, a name tag
  • The chart booklet
  • Access to the self-study modules (in this app) and the logbook
  • The registration form (Meeting 1) or check-in form (Meetings 2 and 3)
  • Copies of the recording forms, handouts and the meeting evaluation
At Meeting 1, type the registration forms into a participant list with full contact details during the day, and give it to everyone by the end of the day. It helps form study groups. Keep a copy.

read.text: Before the day

  • ✔ Sound: test it, so videos are heard throughout the room.

sections.title: Section 1: Welcome and course overview
sections.goal: Open the meeting, set the stage for IMNCI, give out the materials, and explain how the course runs.

read.text: Time: 30 minutes. Introductions, then the course's structure and objectives, and the plan for today.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Materials

  • Slides
  • The self-study materials for each participant (access to the modules in this app, the logbook)
  • Flipchart
1.1 Welcome participants

1. Introduce yourself and your co-facilitators: your clinical background, your IMNCI experience, your experience as a trainer and mentor, and how you will serve as course facilitator.
  2. Invite participants to introduce themselves, and write their names on the flipchart: preferred name, workplace and role, and their hopes for the training (or another icebreaker, such as an interesting fact about themselves).
1.2 Set the stage: why are we here?

IMNCI is a strategy for integrated case management of the most common symptoms and conditions that cause illness and death in children under 5 years. It has been adapted in over 100 countries, and thousands of health workers have been trained. It improves health worker skills, health systems, and family and community practices in child care.
read.label: Say to the group

read.text: This is a 3-month distance course. At home you will study, practise IMNCI in your clinic, and work with mentors and study groups. This group will meet two more times.
read.label: Say to the group

read.text: 1.3 The self-study materials
Explain the purpose of each material, and open it with the participants:

• The modules: open the course in the app on the screen and walk through the module list: Module 1 opens first, each lesson opens when the one before it is finished, and every module ends with a test.
  • The logbook: where participants note exercises and recording forms as they study and practise. You will explain it in detail at the end of the day.
1.4 to 1.7 Course overview

cards.back: Use integrated case management for common problems of sick young infants and children; use the chart booklet and recording forms in practice; counsel caregivers on home treatment, feeding, care of the well child and disease prevention.

Flexibility: study in your own time and save travel, so more health workers are trained. Learner-driven: the meetings focus on the problems you face. It combines 3 meetings, self-study, practice in your own facility, a mentor, and group study.

Orientation (today), self-study period 1 (Modules 1 and 2, 3 to 4 weeks), Review and practice (1 day), self-study period 2 (remaining modules, 6 to 8 weeks), Final synthesis (1 day). Throughout: work with mentors, review with study groups, practise in the clinic with the chart booklet and recording forms.

Time, energy and commitment: you need to be motivated. Practise seeing children with the IMNCI tools. Work with others: colleagues, study groups and mentors. If you do not know something, ASK and seek help.

read.text: Set the tone for the course: hard work, motivation, teamwork and pursuing learning. Answer questions as they come.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: 1.8 Announcements for the day

• Ask the group to set ground rules for the day; write them on the flipchart and put it on the wall.
  • Mobile phones off; use them only in breaks. The day is busy and needs full attention.
  • The meeting runs until 16:30, with breaks in the morning and afternoon and lunch at 12:30.
  • Show the facilities (toilets, phones). Answer administrative questions.
1.9 Reinforce key principles

• Distance learning takes motivation, time and energy.
  • It needs practice in the clinic with the IMNCI tools.
  • Participants involve others: mentors, study group members, colleagues and the in-charge.
  • Much of the learning happens through feedback and solving problems together.
Next we will get a feel for IMNCI and how it can improve your clinical work, and talk about making your clinic welcoming.
read.label: Say to the group

sections.title: Section 2: Creating a welcoming environment
sections.goal: Use a video and discussion to raise interest in IMNCI and show why good communication makes a clinic welcoming.

read.text: Time: 30 minutes. Grab the participants' interest in IMNCI with a video and discussion, and show that what they do with IMNCI matters.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Materials

2.1 Introduction to the IMNCI process

Integrated case management may sound confusing. What matters is that IMNCI has a very specific process that walks you through examining the child, finding the health problems and giving the right treatment.
read.label: Say to the group

read.title: General danger signs: convulsions
read.caption: IMNCI training video, about 4 minutes. Participants open the chart booklet at the sick child chart and take a sick child recording form: these signs are the first box.

read.text: This video is older than the present chart booklet and shows some signs no longer in it. Use it to show the process in a clinic.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: 2.2 Discussion

Write the answers on the flipchart:

  • What did you observe in this video?
  • What does IMNCI help you do in the clinic?
  • When a child enters your clinic, what do you do to make the family feel welcome?
  • What useful examples can you share about creating a welcoming environment?
2.3 Reinforce key principles

• Caregivers are very emotional when a child is sick.
  • Health workers play a critical role in a welcoming environment: be sensitive to the emotional needs and situation of the family and child.
  • Good communication builds rapport and trust, so the caregiver shares more about the illness and the home.
  • Reinforce the good practices shared: open questions, sitting next to the mother, asking her name and situation, listening to her answers.

read.label: The same skills in Module 1
read.text: Participants study greeting the caregiver and the good communication skills here.
Creating a welcoming clinic also gets us better information for case management. Now let us look at what brings these families to our clinics.
read.label: Say to the group

sections.title: Section 3: Causes of childhood illness
sections.goal: Lead a short discussion on why children die, so participants see the problem IMNCI addresses.

read.text: Time: 15 minutes. Data and discussion on the causes of child illness and death. Bring your own expertise, and data for your state or locality.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Emphasize that:

  • Most children die from preventable causes: acute respiratory infection, diarrhoea, malnutrition, measles, malaria, HIV and newborn causes.
  • Children often have overlapping conditions. Malnutrition and HIV are common underlying causes of other illness.
  • Inequity raises child deaths in rural communities and poorer households.

Materials

  • Slides (add slides with national or local data)
  • Flipchart
3.1 What causes illness and death in our children?

Let the group think about what they see in their facilities before showing data, which may surprise them. Draw an empty pie chart on the flipchart and fill in the slices as participants name causes. They will probably be surprised by the proportions.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: 3.2 Comparing our area with global data

Cause of death in children under 5 (WHO, 2010)Share

Acute respiratory infection16%
Diarrhoea10%
Malaria7%
Injury5%

UndernutritionAn underlying cause in up to half of child deaths
How do underlying causes such as malnutrition and HIV add to illness and death?
read.answer: A child missing key nutrients grows poorly, develops poorly and has weaker immunity, so infections are more frequent and more severe. HIV reduces the child's immune function.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: 3.3 Inequity and health

• What affects child health?
  • Children are more likely to die before 5 if they live in poorer households, in rural areas, or have mothers with less education. Why?
  • For those working in towns: how does this relate to your patients?

Factors participants may name: rural transport, fewer clinics in rural areas, access to health information, access to education (especially for women), food insecurity, poverty, women's say in decisions at home, lack of clean water and sanitation.
How would we define inequity?
read.answer: Inequity is the uneven distribution of health caused by conditions that may be avoidable, and that are unjust and unfair: for example, differences in health between social groups.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: 3.5 Key points about child deaths

1. Most children die of preventable causes.
  2. The major killers under 5: newborn conditions (infection, asphyxia, prematurity; low birthweight babies account for 70% of newborn deaths), diarrhoea and pneumonia.
  3. Malnutrition is an underlying cause in up to half of deaths.
  4. HIV is an underlying cause in many countries.
  5. Economic, social, political and cultural factors affect child health. Poorer households and rural communities have higher child mortality; women's education matters.

Children often die from preventable, overlapping causes. Integrated case management examines every child for all the common problems: cough, diarrhoea, fever, ear problems and malnutrition. Next we see how IMNCI does this.
read.label: Say to the group

sections.title: Section 4: The IMNCI process
sections.goal: Define integrated case management, walk through the IMNCI process, and choose the chart by the child's age.

read.text: Time: 60 minutes for the whole of Section 4. This is the most important section of the day: the foundation for the whole course. Participants must be very clear on the IMNCI process and on the chart booklet and recording forms before self-study. Check understanding with questions and examples as you go.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Materials

  • Chart booklets to give out
  • Sick child recording forms, 2 per participant
  • Slides
  • IMNCI training video
  • Flipchart
4.1 Defining IMNCI

IMNCI is the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness. Integrated means we do not look only at one symptom, or only at the problem the parent tells us. If we treat only the diarrhoea, we may miss that the child also has fever and is malnourished. IMNCI assesses every young infant and child for the major causes of illness and death, so we give more complete care and find problems we would otherwise miss.
read.label: Say to the group

read.text: Sudan national booklet: The strategy is called IMNCI (Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness). WHO module (page 46): The strategy is called IMCI.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: 4.2 The IMNCI process

read.title: Seven steps, every time a child under 5 comes to the clinic

steps.title: 1. Greet the caregiver
steps.text: Ask why the child is brought, and whether this is an initial or a follow-up visit.

steps.title: 2. Assess for signs of severe illness
steps.text: A child with these signs needs urgent referral. The signs depend on the age group.

steps.title: 3. Assess the main symptoms
steps.text: Ask the caregiver and make your own observations. The main symptoms differ by age group. You also assess underlying problems such as malnutrition. ASK, LOOK, LISTEN, FEEL: ask about a problem, then look, listen and feel for signs (for example, look whether a child is unconscious, listen for difficult breathing, feel for swelling).

steps.title: 4. Classify and identify treatment
steps.text: Use the charts to classify the severity. Colours are like traffic lights: RED is very serious and needs urgent referral; YELLOW is treated at the health facility; GREEN is treated at home.

steps.title: 5. Treat
steps.text: Treat the child for everything you identified.

steps.title: 6. Counsel
steps.text: Counsel the caregiver on treatment at home, feeding and other care, and on when to come back.

steps.title: 7. Follow-up
steps.text: When the child returns, IMNCI says how to give follow-up care.

read.text: 4.3 The two job aids

1. The chart booklet: the charts with the IMNCI instructions. Tell participants which national edition you use, and its year.
  2. The recording form: for notes as you use the chart booklet.

Share your own experience of using the booklet and form in the clinic; show that they are easy to use. Make sure everyone has a chart booklet and recording forms (one for a sick child, one for a young infant).
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: 4.4 Using the age-appropriate chart
The chart booklet has two sets of charts. Open both with the participants: the sick young infant (up to 2 months) and the sick child (2 months up to 5 years).
What does "up to 5 years" mean?
read.answer: The child has not reached the fifth birthday. The same for "up to 2 months".
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Which chart do you use?

items.text: Had the fifth birthday last month

read.text:
Summarize:

  • The process is the same for both age groups: assess for severe signs, assess the main symptoms, classify and identify treatment, treat, counsel and follow up.
  • The charts are separate because young infants and children differ in the signs you assess and in some treatments.
  • That is why you must find out the child's age straight away.

read.lesson: Introduction to the sick young infant
read.label: Young infant charts: Module 2

sections.title: Section 4: A tour of the chart booklet and recording form
sections.goal: Walk through the chart booklet and recording form step by step, from greeting to follow-up.

read.text: Participants follow in the chart booklet, open at the first sick child chart, and on a sick child recording form.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: 4.5 Greet
Picture a child and mother coming into our clinic room. Before we assess, we need some information, at the top of the chart and of the form.
read.label: Say to the group

steps.title: Greet the child and caregiver
steps.text: Use the tips from the morning on a welcoming environment.

steps.title: The child's age
steps.text: It decides which charts you use.

steps.title: ASK: what are the child's problems?
Initial or follow-up visit?
steps.text: Initial: the first visit for this episode of the illness. Follow-up: seen a few days ago for the same illness; you check whether the treatment is helping. The modules teach follow-up visits.

steps.title: Weight and temperature
steps.text: Record them.

read.caption: Chart booklet: check for general danger signs (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

read.text: 4.6 Assess

The ASSESS column says to check for general danger signs, then assess the main symptoms, starting with cough or difficult breathing. We ASK about symptoms, then LOOK, LISTEN and FEEL to make our own observations.
What is the difference between a symptom and a sign?
read.answer: A symptom is what the child presents with, the complaint the caregiver tells you: fever, diarrhoea, cough. Signs are the smaller pieces of information you assess to find the cause: in cough, for example, fast breathing.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What other signs are in the ASSESS box for cough or difficult breathing?
read.answer: Fast breathing, chest indrawing, stridor and wheezing.
read.label: Practice

read.text: How do you mark the form when a child does or does not have a sign?
read.answer: Circle (or tick) each sign the child has. If the child does not have the sign, mark nothing.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: 4.7 Classify

Use the CLASSIFY column to match the child's signs to a coloured classification: RED needs urgent pre-referral treatment and referral; YELLOW is managed at the health facility; GREEN is managed at home with follow-up.
Classify with the chart. What colour, and what action?
groups: Red: pre-referral treatment and urgent referral
Yellow: treat at the health facility

items.text: Cough: fast breathing, and the child is lethargic
items.why: Lethargy is a general danger sign.

items.text: Diarrhoea: lethargic and a very slow skin pinch
Diarrhoea: restless and irritable, no other sign
items.why: One sign is not enough for SOME DEHYDRATION: NO DEHYDRATION.

items.text: Diarrhoea: restless and irritable, and drinks eagerly

read.text: When do you write the classification?
read.answer: Straight away: classify each symptom and write the classification on the form before you go to the next symptom on the chart and the next part of the form.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: 4.8 Identify treatment
The TREATMENT column gives the treatment for each classification and where it is given: referral, health facility or home. Write it on the back of the recording form.
Cough: if you classify PNEUMONIA, what treatments do you record? And COUGH OR COLD?
read.answer: PNEUMONIA: oral amoxicillin for 5 days; an inhaled bronchodilator for 5 days if wheezing; soothe the throat with a safe remedy; refer for assessment if cough over 2 weeks or recurrent wheeze; advise when to return immediately; follow up in 3 days. COUGH OR COLD: soothe the throat; bronchodilator if wheezing; refer if cough over 2 weeks or recurrent wheeze; advise when to return immediately; follow up in 5 days if not improving.
read.label: Practice

read.text: 4.9 Continue the process

After cough, assess and classify the next main symptom, and so on: diarrhoea, fever, ear problem. Then check malnutrition and anaemia, HIV, consider TB, check immunization, vitamin A and deworming, and ask about other problems. Signs and symptoms are different for young infants.
4.10 Treat
What happens when a child has more than one classification?
read.answer: Look at more than one table. Write all the treatments for each classification on the back of the form, then review them together and decide the treatment for the child: this is integrated treatment.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Some dehydration is yellow. Where do you find what to do?
read.answer: The treatment column says Plan B. Turn to Plan B in the TREAT THE CHILD charts.
read.label: Practice

read.text: 4.11 Counsel the caregiver
The COUNSEL THE MOTHER charts cover home treatment, follow-up, and feeding, care at home and prevention. Write the earliest follow-up date on the back of the form.
4.12 Follow-up care
How do you know when the child should come back?
read.answer: Look at all the classifications and choose the earliest follow-up. The caregiver should also know when to return immediately. At the follow-up visit, use the follow-up box for the previous classification, then reassess fully, on a second recording form marked "follow-up visit".
read.label: Clarify

read.text: 4.13 and 4.14 Annexes of the booklet, and tips for study

• Show what reference material and pictures are at the end of the booklet.
  • Study with the booklet and form open: when reading about diarrhoea, follow it in the chart booklet and on the form.
  • Show these tools to your in-charge, and how you will use them in the clinic.
  • Practise, practise, practise: the more you use them, the faster and surer you become.
  • If it helps, tell the caregiver that you will take notes while you ask questions.

sections.title: Section 4: General danger signs, with Biki
sections.goal: Introduce the four general danger signs, practise them with video and Biki's case, and check understanding of the whole process.

read.text: 4.15 Introducing the general danger signs
The first step in assessing is to look for signs of serious illness that need referral. In the sick child they are called general danger signs. If one or more is present, refer urgently.
read.label: Say to the group

cards.front: Not able to drink or breastfeed
cards.back: The child cannot suck or swallow when offered a drink or breast milk. Ask the mother to describe what happens; if unsure, ask her to offer a drink and watch. A blocked nose can stop sucking: clear it, and if the child then breastfeeds, the sign is absent.

Nothing stays down: no food, fluid or medicine. Ask how often and whether every feed comes back; if unsure, offer a drink and watch. A child who vomits several times but keeps some fluid down does not have this sign.

cards.front: Convulsions in this illness, or convulsing now
cards.back: Arms and legs stiffen as the muscles contract; the child may lose consciousness. Use the local words for convulsions (fits, spasms).

Lethargic: not awake and alert when they should be, drowsy, not interested, may stare blankly. Unconscious: cannot be wakened by touch, shaking or voice. A child may have the eyes open and still be lethargic or unconscious.

read.text: 4.16 and 4.17 Video, then practice

read.title: General danger signs
read.caption: IMNCI training video, about 4 minutes. The sick child chart and form open.

read.title: Assess general condition
read.caption: IMNCI training video, about 6 minutes: decide for four children whether they are lethargic or unconscious. Stop at 4:15 to discuss the answers, then play on.

stages.text: Read aloud slowly (about 2 minutes); participants use a recording form as they would in the clinic. Victoria brings her grandson Biki, 7 months. Temperature 37 °C, weight 9 kg. He is not feeding well. They have been to the clinic before, but this is the first visit for this problem.

His mother has died; Victoria gives him milk. Since this morning he is too weak to take it: his head leans back, he will not open his mouth for the cup, and the milk dribbles onto his face. He does not vomit everything and has had no convulsions.
stages.question: Does Biki have a general danger sign so far?
options: Yes: he is not able to drink
stages.explanation: He cannot take the milk: not able to drink or breastfeed.

stages.text: Sitting on Victoria's lap, Biki looks very tired and lies back in her arms. His eyes follow your hand when you snap your fingers, but when Victoria says "hi baby!" he does not look up at her.
stages.question: What do you record?
stages.explanation: One general danger sign is enough: Biki is not able to drink, so he needs urgent attention and referral. His tiredness should also be checked carefully for lethargy.

read.text: 4.18 Practising the recording form

read.title: How well did the health worker use the form?

cards.front: Form 1: a 6-week-old, weight 3.2 kg, "not feeding well", on the sick child form
cards.back: The wrong form: this is a young infant under 2 months, who shows different signs of severe illness. Also, no name and no temperature recorded. (A trick case: do participants notice the age?)

cards.front: Form 2: Sara, 3 months, temperature 36 °C, general danger signs marked NO
cards.back: The problems are not asked and recorded; no weight; it is unclear which signs were present (circle a sign that is present); the child has a general danger sign but it is marked NO.

read.text: 4.19 Check understanding of the IMNCI process
A lot was covered. Take a few minutes to review the process and clear up confusion before clinical practice. Refer back to the slides or the booklet as needed.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: When do we use IMNCI?
read.answer: For every sick child under 5.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What do we want to know from the caregiver before we assess?
read.answer: The child's name, age and problems, and whether it is an initial or follow-up visit.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Where do you look first when you classify?
read.answer: The SIGNS column of the classification table. If the child has signs in more than one row, classify up to the more severe.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: A child has signs in both the red and the yellow row. How do you classify?
read.answer: Always "classify up" to the more severe: red rather than yellow, yellow rather than green.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: I have assessed and classified cough. What next?
read.answer: Identify the treatments in the classification table and write them on the form, then assess and classify the next symptom. After all of them, decide the treatment for all problems, and where it is given: urgent referral, health facility or home.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What do we do when there is at least one general danger sign?
read.answer: Give the urgent pre-referral treatments in the clinic (the bold treatments in the TREATMENT column), then refer urgently.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: After the main symptoms, what do you check?
read.answer: Malnutrition, anaemia, immunization status, HIV, and any other problems the caregiver mentions.
read.label: Clarify

sections.title: Section 5: Clinical practice
sections.goal: Lead the first clinical session: demonstrate IMNCI with real children, and let participants greet and check general danger signs.

read.text: Time: 60 minutes. The first chance to demonstrate IMNCI with sick children. Spend enough time demonstrating one good case. Use the inpatient ward or outpatient clinic, wherever there are patients. More guidance is in the Annexes (clinical practice sessions).
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Participants should:

  • See demonstrations of using the chart booklet and recording forms with patients
  • Check children for general danger signs
  • Practise greeting a caregiver and getting information about a child
  • Use the chart booklet and recording form with a caregiver
  • See demonstrations with other sick children or young infants: as participants have not yet learned that content, you demonstrate and they follow in the job aids

Materials

  • Participants bring their chart booklets and recording forms (logbook or copies)
  • Anything else the clinical setting needs
Summarize, explain transport and lunch. At lunch, regroup with your co-facilitators, and spend time with participants on their plans for self-study and practice.
read.label: Facilitator tip

sections.title: Section 6: The sick young infant
sections.goal: Show why young infants need special care, how the process differs for them, and why breastfeeding matters.

read.text: Time: 60 minutes. IMNCI for the sick young infant. This section does not cover all of Module 2, which participants finish before the next meeting, but they must leave today understanding the process for both age groups.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Materials

  • Slides
  • IMNCI training video
  • Flipchart
6.1 Welcome back

• What questions came up at lunch?
  • What do you think of IMNCI so far? How will it be useful in your clinic?
Open Module 2. The whole module is the IMNCI process for the sick young infant. You will complete it before our next meeting.
read.label: Say to the group

read.text: 6.2 Why young infants are special
Young infants need special attention. Why?
read.answer: They show illness differently from older children. They become sick and die very quickly from serious bacterial infections, the most common serious illness in the first 2 months, especially in low birthweight infants. Often they have only general signs (poor feeding, reduced movement, fever or low temperature), and each is a sign of very serious illness. Mild chest indrawing is normal (the chest wall is soft): only severe chest indrawing is a sign. Newborns are often sick from labour and delivery: asphyxia, birth trauma, prematurity, early infections such as sepsis after prolonged rupture of membranes.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: 6.3 Important care for young infants

• ✔ Breastfeed exclusively, whenever the infant wants, day and night
  • ✔ Keep the infant warm, skin to skin
  • ✔ Good hygiene: wash hands before holding the infant; keep the cord and its area clean
  • ✔ Immunizations
  • ✔ Seek care immediately for signs of severe disease
6.4 The process with the sick young infant

The steps are the same. Greet, ask the age, initial or follow-up, the problems; measure weight and temperature. Assess for signs of very severe disease (all need urgent referral), then the main problems: jaundice, diarrhoea, the infant's or mother's HIV status, feeding problem and growth, immunization, other problems and the mother's health. Classify red, yellow or green, then treat, counsel and follow up.
6.5 Signs of very severe disease

read.title: Assessment of the sick young infant
read.caption: IMNCI training video, about 14 minutes. It shows older signs than the present chart booklet: watch it for the process of assessing a young infant.

read.text: Classify with the young infant chart

items.why: LOCAL BACTERIAL INFECTION: treat at home with the caregiver.

items.text: 60 breaths per minute or more (counted twice)
items.why: Fast breathing: POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE.
SEVERE DISEASE OR LOCAL INFECTION UNLIKELY: advise home care.

read.text: Sudan national booklet: Fast breathing, low temperature and the other severe signs are classified POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE; yellow palms and soles are SEVERE JAUNDICE, referred urgently, as in Module 2. WHO module (page 66): the facilitator guide's practice answers say "possible severe bacterial infection", "no bacterial infection", and for yellow palms "JAUNDICE, yellow, refer for Hb test".
read.label: Sudan national protocol
The young infant classifications in Module 2

read.text: 6.6 Promoting breastfeeding

Make it personal. Ask who has children, who breastfed or supported a partner or relative, what it was like and where they found help, and what problems mothers bring to their clinic (fear of not enough milk, sore nipples). Breastfeeding is not always easy and natural: it needs a great deal of support.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: Why do health workers have an important role in breastfeeding?
read.answer: Fewer than 40% of infants worldwide are exclusively breastfed. Health workers encourage and support mothers to feed well, and help mothers living with HIV find safe feeding options.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: 6.7 Key points for breastfeeding

cards.back: One of the most effective ways to ensure child survival; all the nutrients for healthy development; antibodies against common illnesses; available and affordable, with health benefits for the mother. Not exclusively breastfeeding contributes to over a million avoidable deaths a year.
Start early, within an hour of birth; breastfeed exclusively until 6 months; on demand, as often as the infant wants, day and night.

cards.front: What does exclusive mean? Can I give water?
cards.back: Breast milk and nothing else: no water.

cards.front: Why is breast milk better than formula?
cards.back: Formula has no antibodies; it risks waterborne disease with unsafe water; bottles need careful cleaning; overdiluting gives poor nutrition; many families cannot get or afford it; and milk supply falls if the infant feeds less, so going back to the breast may not be possible.

read.text: Feeding options for a mother living with HIV are taught in Module 8, following the national guidelines.
read.label: Remember

read.lesson: Feeding options for an HIV-infected mother
read.label: Feeding and HIV: Module 8

read.text: 6.8 Using IMNCI to support infant feeding

read.title: Breastfeeding assessment
read.caption: IMNCI training video, about 9 minutes. Participants follow the breastfeeding assessment in their chart booklet and form. Take questions after.

read.text: 6.9 Reinforce key principles

• The process is the same as for the sick child, with the signs that are most common and serious in young infants.
  • Young infants can die quickly from infection and show illness differently.
  • Assessing feeding, positioning and attachment, and counselling on feeding problems, is a major part of IMNCI for the young infant.
  • Breastfeeding is vital for growth and development, and needs support from family and health workers.

sections.title: Section 7: Communication and counselling skills
sections.goal: Teach the APAC process, the three teaching steps and checking questions, and show them in practice.

read.text: Time: 75 minutes, with tea midway (30 + 15 + 30). Explain good communication and counselling skills with concrete examples from the clinic, then reinforce them with a video or facilitator role plays. Participant role plays are optional.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Materials

  • Slides
  • Flipchart
  • For role plays: the handouts (Annexes), one sick child and one young infant recording form per group, props (a cup, a rolled blanket as a baby)
7.1 Why communication matters
Why are good communication skills important to integrated case management?
read.answer: They create a welcoming environment, build trust and rapport, get the information you need by asking the right questions and listening, and let you advise and counsel families on care.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: 7.2 The APAC process

steps.title: ASK and listen
steps.text: Ask questions to find the child's problems; listen to learn what the caregiver already does, what she does well and what needs to change.

steps.title: PRAISE
steps.text: Praise something helpful she has done. Praise must be genuine: only for what really helps the child.

steps.title: ADVISE
steps.text: Some advice is simple (return in 2 days); some means teaching her to do something, with the three teaching steps.

steps.title: CHECK understanding
steps.text: Ask questions to be sure she understood, and explain again if needed.

read.text: 7.3 Teaching a caregiver

steps.title: 1. Give information
steps.text: Explain how to do it: apply eye ointment, prepare ORS, soothe a sore throat. Use words she understands; focus on the most important messages.

steps.title: 2. Show an example
steps.text: Do it yourself: mix ORS, hold the child and apply the ointment. Use real objects or pictures and common teaching aids.

steps.title: 3. Let her practise
steps.text: She does it while you watch and give feedback. This is the most important step: she is more likely to remember what she has practised, and you see what she finds difficult. Answer questions calmly and reassure her.

read.text: 7.4 Checking that a caregiver understands
Ask questions to find what she understands and what needs more explanation. If the answer is unclear, ask another checking question. Praise correct understanding. Explain more if needed.

Good checking questions start with how, why, what, when or where. They are open: they cannot be answered yes or no, and they do not lead to the right answer ("you will remember to wash your hands, won't you?").
read.label: Remember

read.text: Is this a good checking question?

items.text: How much extra fluid will you give after each loose stool?
Will you remember to wash your hands?
Where on the eye will you put the ointment?

read.text:
• Pause, and give her time to answer. Do not rush or give the answer: she may be shy of authority or afraid of being wrong. Encourage her.
  • If she answers wrongly, do not make her uncomfortable. Teach again with information, an example and practice.
7.5 Demonstrating good communication

read.title: Good communication skills: making things clear
read.caption: About 13 minutes. Two scenes in a clinic: first a health worker who uses few of these skills, then a better consultation, each followed by comments. Participants note what the health worker does well and could improve.

read.text: Instead of, or as well as, the video, two facilitators can play the three short scenes in the Annexes (facilitator role plays).
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: What communication skills have we learned so far?
read.answer: APAC (ask and listen, praise, advise, check understanding); the three teaching steps (give information, show an example, let her practise); good checking questions; and useful tips: simple words, common teaching aids, reassurance, praise for correct answers and good practice, invite and answer all questions, focus on the important messages without overloading.
read.label: Practice

sections.title: Section 7: Role plays
sections.goal: Run the three participant role plays in groups of three, and lead the discussion on how well each health worker did.

read.text: The role plays practise communication skills and the IMNCI process, and give constructive feedback to each other.

steps.title: Groups of three
steps.text: Each brings the chart booklet, recording forms and notebook. Give each group one copy of handouts A, B and C, and one sick child and one young infant recording form.

steps.title: Three roles, rotated
steps.text: Health worker: assess the child with good communication and counsel the caregiver. Caregiver: gives information only when asked; this tests whether the health worker asks the right questions. Observer: notes how well the health worker uses the IMNCI process.

steps.title: Timing
steps.text: 10 minutes each: 5 to play and 5 to discuss. Give a one-minute warning and say when to switch roles. Each group does all three.

steps.title: Monitoring
steps.text: Facilitators move between groups and join the discussions. Keep the discussion questions on the screen.

read.text:
Discussion questions for each role play

  1. Did the health worker get all the important information?
  2. Did the health worker use APAC, the three teaching steps, and checking questions?
  3. Caregiver: what did the health worker do well? What could be improved?
  4. Observer: what did the health worker do well? What could be improved?
  5. Health worker: what would you do differently next time?

stages.text: Jon, a boy of 12 months, initial visit, temperature 37 °C, weight 10 kg. A cough for 3 to 4 days, getting worse. He can drink, is not vomiting, has had no convulsions, and is not lethargic. You count 48 breaths per minute and see chest indrawing.
stages.question: How do you classify Jon?
options: SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE (red)
stages.explanation: 48 breaths a minute is fast breathing at 12 months (40 or more), and he has chest indrawing, with no general danger sign and no stridor: PNEUMONIA, treated with oral amoxicillin at the health facility and home, follow-up in 3 days.

read.text: Sudan national booklet: Chest indrawing without a general danger sign or stridor is PNEUMONIA (yellow), with oral amoxicillin, as in Module 3. WHO module (page 76): the facilitator guide's answer slide gives "VERY SEVERE PNEUMONIA, red, urgent referral", from older charts in which chest indrawing meant severe pneumonia.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

stages.text: Amira, 4 weeks, initial visit, temperature 38 °C, weight 3 kg. She seems feverish and very unhappy; she can breastfeed and has had no convulsions. 53 breaths a minute; chest indrawing; she moves only when stimulated. No bulging fontanelle, no nasal flaring or grunting, no umbilical redness, skin pustules or eye discharge, no jaundice.
stages.question: How do you classify Amira?
options: POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE (red)
SEVERE DISEASE OR LOCAL INFECTION UNLIKELY (green)
stages.explanation: Fever (37.5 °C or above) and movement only when stimulated are signs of very severe disease. Give the pre-referral treatment, refer urgently, and counsel the mother to keep Amira warm on the way to hospital and to keep breastfeeding.

read.text: Role play C: the infant has a LOCAL BACTERIAL INFECTION of the umbilicus (it is red). The health worker uses the COUNSEL charts to teach the mother to treat it at home: wash hands, gently clean off pus with soap and water, dry, paint with gentian violet, wash hands again, twice daily for 5 days. Watch for APAC, the three teaching steps and checking questions. The caregiver does nothing until asked: she does not offer to practise unless invited.
read.label: Role play C

read.lesson: Local infections the caregiver can treat at home
read.label: Treating local infections at home: Module 2

read.text: 7.7 Reinforce key principles
Why are communication skills important when using IMNCI?
read.answer: Integrated case management depends on getting full information from the caregiver to assess and classify. Communication lets us counsel well on home treatment, feeding, follow-up and prevention. A welcomed, less anxious caregiver trusts us and remembers the advice. We know from our own lives that it is hard when a child is sick.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Why is praise important?
read.answer: It reinforces good practices and builds rapport with the caregiver.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Close by asking three people for a good checking question and two for a poor one.
read.label: Facilitator tip

sections.title: Section 8: Next steps and closing
sections.goal: Make sure everyone knows what to do in self-study period 1, has a study group and a mentor, and evaluate the day.

read.text: Time: 45 minutes. Review the course calendar and set the next steps. Participants must leave clear about Modules 1 and 2, clinical practice and recording forms, mentors and the in-charge.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Materials

  • Slides
  • The meeting evaluation form (Annexes)
8.1 Review the course materials

• The modules: read everything. A case runs through each module to apply the material to one child. Do the exercises as you read, honestly, without looking for the answers; then check yourself.
  • The logbook: do the module exercises after finishing each module, from memory, without the module open. At least 2 recording forms per module from cases in your clinic. Tick the checklist of clinical signs you see.
  • Bring the logbook to every meeting. The exercises and recording forms count for about a third of the course mark.
The module tests are taken in the app, from memory, after each module. Recording forms from the clinic are still brought to the meeting.
read.label: In this app

read.text: 8.2 Prepare for self-study period 1

• ✔ Read and study Modules 1 and 2
  • ✔ Do the exercises in the modules as you read
  • ✔ Do the logbook exercises after each module
  • ✔ Practise IMNCI in the clinic with recording forms
  • ✔ Meet the study group as often as possible
  • ✔ Work with an IMNCI mentor on problems and questions
  • ✔ Make a study schedule and keep it where you study
Fill in the dates and places of Meetings 2 and 3 with the participants.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: 8.3 Mentors and the in-charge

• Debrief the in-charge officer about the course and how IMNCI will be used in the clinic.
  • Identify a mentor: someone willing to demonstrate IMNCI skills and help apply them; a senior health worker at the hospital or facility, or a colleague trained in IMNCI.
  • Tell participants how you will stay in touch and when you can be reached.
8.4 and 8.5 Study groups and study plans

Tips for study groups

  • Agree regular dates and times
  • Set detailed reading goals
  • Read and do the exercises before the meeting
  • Note what you find confusing and bring questions
  • Talk about cases you have seen
  • Practise together in the clinic

A personal study plan

  • Mark the next meeting, study group meetings and anything that will disrupt study (travel).
  • Set weekly goals: which lessons, when to do recording forms in the clinic, when to do the module tests.
  • Write the plan down and put it where you study.

Set reading goals for this first period: many participants struggle to finish Module 2. Arrange study groups by place and facility; give 10 to 15 minutes for groups to meet, exchange contacts and plan their dates.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text:
WeekSample personal study plan
1Module 1, its test, and 2 recording forms
2Module 2: the sick young infant up to treating (lessons 1 to 13)
3Module 2: follow-up and feeding (lessons 14 to 22), and 2 recording forms
4Module 2: the rest, and its test
8.6 What to bring to Meeting 2

• ✔ Access to the modules
  • ✔ The logbook (and the Module 1 and 2 tests done)
  • ✔ 4 recording forms from clinical practice (2 for each of Modules 1 and 2)
  • ✔ Your questions: difficult cases and confusing material
8.7 and 8.8 Evaluation and close

1. Lead a short discussion for feedback on the day's content, presentation and clarity, before the written evaluation.
  2. Give out the evaluation form. As participants finish, check that each feels ready for self-study.
  3. Close with thanks and energy for the coming three months. Give out the participant contact list, and say how to reach you.

sections.title: Meeting 2 at a glance
sections.goal: See the objectives, place and agenda of the Review and practice meeting.

read.text: Meeting 2 checks the participants' progress in self-study period 1, deals with their difficulties, and introduces the remaining modules. The afternoon is less structured, so that you can give more explanation or practice where it is needed.
By the end of the meeting, participants will:

• Show the skills of Modules 1 and 2 in a clinical setting
  • Explain and show how to use the IMNCI charts to assess, classify and treat the main symptoms and conditions of a sick child: cough or difficult breathing, diarrhoea, fever, malnutrition and anaemia
  • Plan self-study, group study, work with mentors and clinical practice for the remaining modules
Hold this meeting on site, so that you practise together in a clinic: at the district hospital, a central health facility, or during site visits.
