sections.title: Sections 1 and 2: Welcome back, and review of self-study period 1
sections.goal: Welcome the group back, then review the logbooks and lead the plenary on how self-study went.

read.text: Time: 15 minutes for Section 1. Re-introductions, the course structure (what is done, what comes next), and today's objectives and agenda.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
1. Re-introduce yourself and your co-facilitators.
  2. Participants re-introduce themselves on the flipchart: name, workplace and role, and one thing they have found especially useful about IMNCI so far.
  3. Summarize what they said about the benefits of the course.
  4. Review the course objectives and structure, and today's agenda: self-study review in the morning, clinical practice late morning, the main symptoms of the coming modules in the afternoon. It is a busy day: it needs discipline to stay on task.

Today is the time to raise what you found hard: do not be afraid to ask. Self-study only gets harder if you carry confusion about IMNCI into it. Share your experience of practising IMNCI, and learn from each other's good practices.
read.label: Say to the group

read.text: Section 2: Reviewing self-study period 1

Time: 45 minutes. A critical chance to see (a) how well participants use IMNCI in their practice, (b) how well they understand Modules 1 and 2, and (c) any big problems with the course arrangements: self-study, study groups, mentors.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text: Split the work. One facilitator leads the plenary discussion; the others collect the logbooks and recording forms, mark them for completeness, note common problems to discuss with the group, and give them back. The answer keys are in this guide, under Following each module.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: Before the meeting, look at each learner's progress and test results for Modules 1 and 2 in the app. Bring a list of who has not finished, and the questions most people got wrong.
read.label: In this app

read.text: 2.2 Plenary: our reflections on self-study

Look for problem areas in content, self-study and practice. Before you answer a question, invite other participants to answer, share experience or solve it together. Note the key points on the flipchart.
read.label: Facilitator tip

cards.back: What was it like to read and do the exercises in Module 1? Module 2? What parts were most useful (exercises, cases)? Who will share a practice that helped them study?
What was hard in Module 1? Module 2? What can we discuss and explain together now?
How did you use IMNCI in the clinic? How did you use the chart booklet and recording forms? What is hard about bringing Modules 1 and 2 into the clinic? Where are you stuck?
What hard cases did you see? Who will walk us through a case and its recording form?
How did the study groups go? Who are your mentors, how have you reached them, and how will they help? Who will share how they told their in-charge or colleagues about the course?

read.text: 2.3 Addressing the problems from the logbooks

The facilitators who reviewed the logbooks now take the problem areas they found, with the flipchart or slides. Close by summarizing the problems and the solutions the group reached, and praise good practices.

sections.title: Section 3: Cough and diarrhoea
sections.goal: Introduce assessing and classifying cough or difficult breathing and diarrhoea, so participants can look for them in the clinic.

read.text: Time: 45 minutes. A short introduction to the first two main symptoms, so they can be included in the clinical practice. Participants learn them fully in Modules 3 and 4. If time is short, show only one of the two videos; participants watch the other at home.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Materials

  • IMNCI training video
  • Slides
3.1 Refresh: IMNCI for the sick child
What do we want to find out when we greet the caregiver?
read.answer: The child's age; whether this is an initial or follow-up visit; the child's problems; weight and temperature.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Without looking: what are the general danger signs?
read.answer: Not able to drink or breastfeed; vomits everything; convulsions (in this illness, or convulsing now); lethargic or unconscious.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What do we do for a red classification?
read.answer: Give the urgent pre-referral treatments, then refer urgently.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Ask one participant to walk the group through the steps: assess and classify the main symptoms and other conditions, identify treatment, treat in the clinic or advise home treatment, counsel the caregiver, and give follow-up care.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: 3.2 Signs of cough or difficult breathing
Open the chart booklet at the cough or difficult breathing chart, and ask questions that make participants read it.
What do we ASK?
read.answer: Does the child have cough or difficult breathing? For how long?
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What do we LOOK and LISTEN for?
read.answer: Count the breaths in one minute; look for chest indrawing; look and listen for stridor and wheezing. The child must be calm.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What is fast breathing?
read.answer: 2 months up to 12 months: 50 breaths per minute or more. 12 months up to 5 years: 40 breaths per minute or more.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: The WHO facilitator guide's answer here has the two cut-offs the wrong way round. Use the cut-offs above, as in the chart booklet and Module 3.
read.label: Correction

read.text: Describe where to watch when counting breaths, what chest indrawing looks like, and how stridor and wheezing sound: give examples from your own practice (how harsh stridor sounds).
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.lesson: Count the breaths: does the child have fast breathing?
read.label: Counting breaths in Module 3
Chest indrawing, stridor and wheezing in Module 3

read.text: 3.3 Signs of diarrhoea
What do we ASK?
read.answer: Does the child have diarrhoea? For how long? Is there blood in the stool?
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What do we LOOK and FEEL for?
read.answer: The general condition: lethargic or unconscious, or restless and irritable; sunken eyes; offer fluid: not able to drink or drinking poorly, or drinking eagerly, thirsty; pinch the skin of the abdomen: does it go back very slowly (longer than 2 seconds) or slowly?
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Why do we pinch the skin?
read.answer: To assess dehydration: the skin of a dehydrated child goes back slowly. Show how: pinch the skin of the abdomen halfway between the umbilicus and the side, lengthwise, for one second, then release and watch.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Ask how they would describe blood in the stool to a caregiver who is unsure, and answer questions on lethargy, restlessness and how the child drinks.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.title: Assess and classify diarrhoea
read.caption: IMNCI training video, about 9 minutes. Stop at each stage to show how it follows the chart booklet and the form.

read.title: Cough or difficult breathing
read.caption: IMNCI training video, about 12 minutes. Stop at each stage to show how it follows the chart booklet and the form.

read.lesson: Look for dehydration: condition, eyes and drinking
read.label: Signs of dehydration in Module 4

read.lesson: The skin pinch, and assessing Mary
read.label: The skin pinch in Module 4

read.text: 3.4 Before clinical practice

• ✔ Bring chart booklets and recording forms
  • ✔ Explain the move, and the need to keep time
  • ✔ Where you will see patients (outpatient, inpatient), and how
  • ✔ What is expected of participants
  • ✔ When the group meets again for lunch

sections.title: Section 4: Clinical practice
sections.goal: Demonstrate a full assessment, then let each participant practise and receive feedback.

read.text: Time: 90 minutes in the clinic. Demonstrate a sick young infant and/or a sick child: assess and classify general danger signs, cough or difficult breathing, or diarrhoea. Then, by time and patients, either keep demonstrating with participants' input, or assign participants alone or in groups and observe and mentor. More guidance in the Annexes.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Participants should:

  • See a sick young infant assessed, if one is available
  • See a sick child assessed, classified, treated and counselled for cough or difficult breathing or diarrhoea
  • Practise greeting a caregiver and getting information, and checking general danger signs
  • Assess, classify, treat and counsel cough, diarrhoea, and sick young infants
  • Use the chart booklet and recording form with a caregiver
Every participant receives at least one piece of feedback from a facilitator on a case: use of the chart booklet, the classification, the treatment and the counselling.
read.label: Remember

read.text: At lunch, regroup with co-facilitators, and spend time with participants on their self-study and practice.
read.label: Facilitator tip

sections.title: Section 5: Fever
sections.goal: Introduce fever and measles: why they matter, how to assess, and how to classify.

read.text: Time: 75 to 90 minutes for the whole of Section 5, with tea. Introduce the modules of period 2: fever, malnutrition and anaemia, and the other modules. Show how each fits integrated management. For each: why it matters, the ASSESS box, the signs used to CLASSIFY, and the TREAT and COUNSEL charts, with your own experience.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text: 5.1 Assessing fever
What can cause fever in children?
read.answer: Mainly malaria, measles and other infections.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: How do we decide a child has fever?
read.answer: By history, feeling hot, or a temperature of 37.5 °C or above.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Sudan national booklet: Test every child with fever (and no general danger sign or stiff neck) for malaria. WHO module (page 99): the guide asks whether the area is high malaria risk (more than 5% of fevers in children due to malaria) or low risk, and the module tests only some fevers in low-risk areas.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: What do we ASK?
read.answer: Does the child have fever? For how long? If more than 7 days, has fever been present every day? Has the child had measles in the last 3 months?
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What do we LOOK and FEEL for?
read.answer: Stiff neck; runny nose; signs of measles: a generalized rash and one of cough, runny nose or red eyes. Do a malaria test.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: If the child has measles now or in the last 3 months, what do we LOOK for?
read.answer: Mouth ulcers (deep and extensive?), pus draining from the eye, clouding of the cornea.
read.label: Clarify

read.title: Assess and classify fever
read.caption: IMNCI training video, about 9 minutes, optional. Its signs are older than the chart booklet.

read.lesson: Assess fever: history, stiff neck and the malaria test
read.label: Assessing fever in Module 5

sections.title: Section 5: Malnutrition and anaemia
sections.goal: Demonstrate weighing, measuring, the z-score and MUAC, practise plotting, and introduce anaemia.

read.text: 5.2 Checking for malnutrition and anaemia

Undernutrition is an underlying cause in up to half of child deaths. Assess every child for malnutrition and anaemia: the signs are easy for us and for the caregiver to miss, and even mild and moderate malnutrition raises the risk of illness and death.
read.label: Say to the group

read.text: Why are children malnourished?
read.answer: Not enough food, poor use of nutrients, and infections. Poor nutrition affects growth and development.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What do we LOOK and measure?
read.answer: Oedema of both feet; weight-for-height (or length) as a z-score; and MUAC. There are separate charts for boys and girls.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Demonstrate the measurements
These are often done wrongly. Demonstrate each, and how to read the result.
read.label: Facilitator tip

steps.title: Weight
steps.text: The right scale and where to place it; a child who can stand; a small child who cannot.

steps.title: Length
steps.text: Lying down, for a child under 2 years or a weak child.

steps.title: Height
steps.text: Standing, for a child of 2 years and older.

steps.title: Weight-for-height or length
steps.text: Find the z-score on the chart for the child's sex: you need the weight in kg and the height or length in cm.

steps.title: MUAC
steps.text: Show it with a MUAC tape, on a child of 6 months or older.

read.text: Who will explain how to find weight-for-height? And how to measure MUAC?
read.answer: Let two participants explain, then correct and complete.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Practise plotting on the chart

read.title: A girl, 105 cm, 13.5 kg
read.text: Plot her on the weight-for-height chart and read the z-score.
read.explanation: She lies below the -2 line and above -3: between -3 and -2 z.

read.title: A girl, 80 cm, 10 kg
read.text: She is 18 months old, so use the weight-for-length chart.
read.explanation: She is between the median and -1: -2 z or more.

read.title: A boy, 118 cm, 16 kg
read.text: Plot him on the weight-for-height chart.
read.explanation: He is below the -3 line: less than -3 z.

read.title: A boy, 100 cm, 13 kg
read.text: Plot him on the weight-for-height chart.
read.explanation: He is just below the -2 line: between -3 and -2 z.

read.lesson: Weight-for-height or length, and the z-score
read.label: The z-score in Module 6

read.text: Anaemia
What is anaemia?
read.answer: Too few red blood cells for the body's needs. Causes: infections, malaria, worms that cause blood loss from the gut (such as hookworm), and lack of iron, vitamin B12, folate or vitamin A. Iron deficiency is among the most common.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What do we LOOK for?
read.answer: Palmar pallor.
read.label: Clarify

read.title: Assess for malnutrition, anaemia and ear problems
read.caption: IMNCI training video, about 8 minutes, optional.

sections.title: Section 5: Ear problems, HIV and the well child
sections.goal: Introduce the other modules of period 2: ear problems, HIV/AIDS and care of the well child.

read.text: 5.3 Ear problems
What do we ASK?
read.answer: Does the child have an ear problem? Ear pain? Ear discharge, and for how long?
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What do we LOOK and FEEL for?
read.answer: Pus seen draining from the ear; tender swelling behind the ear.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Ear problems are so common: why worry about them?
read.answer: They can cause ear damage and deafness, and serious infection.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What is mastoiditis?
read.answer: An infection of the mastoid bone behind the ear: tender swelling behind the ear. It is red and needs urgent referral.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: 5.4 Introduction to HIV

Fit this introduction to the national policy and priorities. In many countries HIV adds greatly to child deaths and underlies malnutrition, pneumonia and diarrhoea; testing, early infant diagnosis and treatment for children have low coverage, and children are lost to follow-up.
read.label: Facilitator tip

cards.back: Because you assess every child you see.
It says when children should start ART at primary care level.
It guides the management of common problems in HIV-infected children, quickly, including opportunistic infections and nutrition.
At primary care level, so children are not lost.

read.text: Why is HIV care in children different from adults?
read.answer: HIV can progress very quickly in children, so early identification, prophylaxis, rapid treatment of opportunistic infections and starting ART when needed are critical. Testing methods differ, ART formulations differ, and children need special care to grow and develop well.
read.label: Clarify

cards.back: Detect HIV antibodies, which pass from mother to child and can remain until 18 months. A positive test under 18 months only shows the child is HIV-exposed; it does not confirm infection.
Detect the virus itself. A positive test at any age confirms infection. If the child is breastfeeding, a negative test does not exclude infection: repeat it 6 weeks after breastfeeding stops.

read.lesson: Read a test result under 18 months
read.label: Early infant diagnosis: Module 8

read.text:
Prophylaxis and treatment

  • ARV prophylaxis given to exposed infants from birth helps prevent HIV infection.
  • Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis reduces illness and death from PCP and common bacterial infections: for HIV-exposed infants from 4 to 6 weeks, and for children with HIV infection.
  • Isoniazid preventive therapy prevents TB in children living with HIV.
  • Exposed and infected children follow the same immunization and vitamin A schedule.
  • ART does not cure HIV, but prevents damage to the immune system and improves quality of life and life expectancy. Three drugs, with strict adherence, reduce drug resistance.
  • All children with confirmed HIV infection are eligible for ART. The steps: confirm infection; make sure the caregiver can give ART; decide whether ART can start at this level; record the baseline on the treatment card; start ART and cotrimoxazole.
The first-line regimens and doses have changed since 2014. Use Module 8 and the current national HIV guidelines, not the regimens on the 2014 slides.
read.label: Changed since 2014

read.lesson: Starting ART: baseline, regimen and dose
read.label: Starting ART: Module 8

read.text: ART dosing exercise: participants find the ART dosing tables, prepare the dose of each drug in the combination with the medicines provided, and call a facilitator to check. You can also role-play teaching a caregiver to give ART: information, demonstration, practice with feedback.
5.5 Introduction to care of the well child

Until now IMNCI has been about sick children. Module 9 is about the well child who comes to the clinic: an area many health workers were never trained in, with a large effect on health and development.
read.label: Say to the group

cards.back: Physical growth, changes in body and strength. Monitored by regular weight and height or length.
Mental, creative, social and adaptive skills. Monitored by milestones, play and communication.
Bonding between mother and child; caregivers who notice and respond to the child; communication; play with homemade or cheap items; watching milestones.
Accidents (poisoning, road, drowning, falls, burns), immunization, regular vitamin A and deworming.

read.text: How would you use the care for child development chart in your clinic?
read.answer: Participants do not know it yet: the question gets them thinking. Share your own experience, and invite theirs.
read.label: Clarify

sections.title: Section 6: Integrated treatment, counselling and follow-up
sections.goal: Reinforce integrated treatment, run the dosing activity, review counselling skills and follow-up care.

read.text: Time: 30 minutes. The day has been about assessing and classifying. This section makes participants confident to use the whole IMNCI process in their own clinics: treat, counsel and follow up.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Materials

  • Slides
  • Flipchart
  • A tray of medicines, prepared beforehand
  • The dosing worksheet (Annexes)
6.1 Integrated treatment

stages.text: Sam has no general danger sign. He is classified PNEUMONIA and ACUTE EAR INFECTION.
stages.question: What antibiotic does he need?
options: Oral amoxicillin, one course, for 5 days
Two antibiotics, one for each classification
stages.explanation: Both classifications are treated with oral amoxicillin, so one course treats both. Never double the dose or lengthen the course because two classifications need the same antibiotic.

stages.text: Where is he treated, and what else does he need?
stages.question: Which is right?
options: At the health facility and home: amoxicillin, paracetamol for ear pain, dry the ear by wicking, a soothing remedy for the cough
stages.explanation: Both classifications are yellow: start treatment at the health facility, continue at home. Counsel on giving amoxicillin at home, wicking, the soothing remedy, and when to return immediately.

stages.question: Follow-up in:
stages.explanation: PNEUMONIA: 3 days; ACUTE EAR INFECTION: 5 days. Choose the earliest: 3 days. At the follow-up visit, use the follow-up boxes for each classification, then reassess fully.

read.text: Sudan national booklet: Pneumonia and acute ear infection are both treated with oral amoxicillin, and dysentery with ciprofloxacin. WHO module (page 112): the guide's example uses cotrimoxazole as first line for acute ear infection and dysentery, from older charts.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: 6.2 Giving antibiotics

• The schedule says how many days and how many times a day. Most antibiotics are given for 5 days.
  • To find the dose: the column for the tablet or syrup your clinic has, the row for the child's weight (better than age); the dose is where they meet.
  • When possible, choose one antibiotic that treats all the child's illnesses.
  • Do not double the dose or lengthen the course because two illnesses need the same antibiotic.
  • Sometimes two antibiotics are needed: a child with DYSENTERY and PNEUMONIA receives ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin.
What treatments are given at home?
read.answer: Oral medicines and treatment of local infections. They depend on good counselling.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: 6.3 Treatments given in the clinic
What are the treatments in bold?
read.answer: The urgent pre-referral treatments, given at the health facility before referral.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Examples of treatments given in the clinic?
read.answer: An intramuscular antibiotic if the child cannot take oral medicine; diazepam for convulsions; IM quinine before referral for severe febrile disease; breast milk or sugar water to prevent low blood sugar; the first doses of oral treatments.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: 6.4 Activity: preparing doses

steps.title: Take the worksheet
steps.text: Each child on it has an age and weight.

steps.title: Prepare each dose
steps.text: From the medicines on the tray, and put it in the box on the worksheet. For intramuscular medicines, dilute the powder with sterile water and draw up the right amount in the right syringe.

steps.title: Call a facilitator
steps.text: To check your doses when you are ready.

read.text: Do any of the medicines look alike? How do we avoid confusing them, for ourselves and for caregivers?
read.answer: Point out tablets that look similar and could be confused when more than one is dispensed; label clearly and show the caregiver each one.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: 6.5 Counselling the caregiver
What do we counsel caregivers on?
read.answer: Home treatment, feeding, keeping an infant warm, preparing ORS, when to return.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What are the three teaching steps, and what matters in each?
read.answer: Give information (simple words, not too much at once); show an example (with things found at home); let her practise (praise, give feedback, more practice if needed). Then check understanding with open questions: why, how, when, where.
read.label: Clarify

read.title: When there is a lot to say: give the most important advice

cards.back: How much can this caregiver understand and remember? Will she come back for follow-up, so some advice can wait? What advice matters most to get the child well?
Antibiotics, antimalarials, fluids for diarrhoea: what the child's survival depends on.
The feeding assessment and counselling, soothing remedies, iron treatment, and similar.

read.text: 6.6 Follow-up care

steps.title: The condition
steps.text: Is it improving, the same, or worse? Use the follow-up box for the earlier classification.

steps.title: Reassess
steps.text: Check the child for any new symptoms or conditions.

steps.title: A new recording form
steps.text: Marked FOLLOW-UP VISIT.

read.text: Time: 15 minutes for Section 1. Re-introductions, the course objectives, and the day, especially the assessments.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
1. Re-introduce yourself and your co-facilitators.
  2. Participants re-introduce themselves on the flipchart: name, one way the course has changed how they practise, and one challenge or question from practising IMNCI.
  3. Summarize the benefits they describe.
  4. Review the course objectives: how do they feel about each? Where do they feel weak?
  5. Review the day: the morning reviews self-study, with each participant meeting a facilitator about their logbook and practice; late morning is clinical practice; the afternoon is the skills stations and the written examination; the day ends with the certificates.

Today is the last chance to raise what you find hard, and to review integrated case management together. In the afternoon you are assessed on your skills (stations and examination), and on your logbook and recording forms.

read.text: Section 2: Reviewing self-study period 2
Time: 45 minutes. As at Meeting 2: one facilitator leads the plenary while the others review and mark the logbooks and recording forms.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text: Check each learner's progress and test results for Modules 3 to 9 in the app before the meeting. The tests stand in for the logbook exercises.

cards.back: Who will share a practice that helped them study?
What was hard in Module 3? 4? 5? 6? The others?
How did you use IMNCI in the clinic? Where are you stuck?
Who will walk us through a case and its recording form?
How did the study groups go? How did you work with mentors?

read.text: Where a clear problem appears, show a video or explain the content then. Close by summarizing the problems, the solutions, and anything still open; praise the efforts to use IMNCI in practice.

sections.title: Section 3: Reviewing integrated case management
sections.goal: Practise the whole process on a video case and a written case before clinical practice.

read.text: Time: 30 minutes. Practise the complete process before the clinical session and the assessments. Push the participants. Use the cases to revisit any problem area from Section 2.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Materials

  • IMNCI training video
  • Slides
  • Sick child recording forms (one for each case)
3.1 Video case: Martha

read.title: Summary case study: Martha
read.caption: IMNCI training video, about 17 minutes. Participants follow with the chart booklet and a recording form. Stop before the classifications to discuss, then play them. Parts of the assessment are out of date.

read.text:
• How did you classify Martha?
  • What treatments were identified?
  • What integrated treatment do you recommend?
  • How will you counsel the caregiver?
  • When should she come back for follow-up, and what will you do then?
3.2 Written case: Kali (optional)

stages.text: Kali, 7 months, 7 kg, is coughing and seems very sick. She has no general danger sign, no fever and no ear problem. She has cough with fast breathing, no chest indrawing, no stridor or wheeze. She has had diarrhoea for 5 days, without blood, with sunken eyes and a slow skin pinch. No pallor.
stages.question: How do you classify Kali?
stages.explanation: Fast breathing: PNEUMONIA. Two signs of dehydration (sunken eyes, slow skin pinch): SOME DEHYDRATION. Five days is not persistent diarrhoea.

stages.question: What is her treatment?
options: Oral amoxicillin for 5 days, and Plan B with zinc
stages.explanation: Amoxicillin for PNEUMONIA (7 kg: 1 tablet of 250 mg, or 5 ml of 250 mg/5 ml syrup, twice daily for 5 days), and Plan B: ORS in the clinic over 4 hours, then reassess; zinc for 14 days. Teach the mother: give information, show how, let her practise. Label the medicine envelope with the dose and times.

stages.question: When should Kali come back for follow-up?
stages.explanation: PNEUMONIA: follow up in 3 days (the earliest of her classifications). Return immediately if she is not able to drink or breastfeed, becomes sicker, develops fever, has fast or difficult breathing, has blood in the stool, or drinks poorly.

read.text: The WHO guide's answer gives follow-up in 2 days. Pneumonia is followed up in 3 days in the chart booklet and Module 3.
read.label: Correction

read.text: Ask each participant to write three checking questions for Kali's mother about the oral medicines, and discuss them.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.lesson: Treat: Plan B at the clinic
read.label: Plan B in Module 4

sections.title: Section 4: Clinical practice
sections.goal: Observe each participant doing full assessments, and give concrete feedback.

read.text: Time: 90 minutes in the clinic. The last chance to watch participants use IMNCI in the clinic. Observe them doing full assessments: one to one, or in groups where participants take turns and the others observe. The session should show full understanding of the process and all the main symptoms. Where you see gaps, demonstrate good practice. More in the Annexes.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Participants should:

  • Do full IMNCI assessments of sick young infants, if available
  • Do full assessments of sick children with all the main symptoms
  • Use the IMNCI charts and recording forms well
  • Receive concrete feedback from facilitators or peers: every participant
Using IMNCI with HIV is hard in this short session: most clinics lack the private space needed. Review HIV in self-study practice, ideally with a mentor or a visiting facilitator.
read.label: HIV

sections.title: Section 5: Skills stations
sections.goal: Run 2 to 4 skills stations, keep the room quiet, and mark the answer sheets.

read.text: Time: 75 minutes. The first part of the assessment. Choose 2 to 4 stations by time and by whether there is power. The answer sheets and keys are in the Annexes; punch out the correct answers on a key to mark quickly.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.title: Two ways to run the stations

cards.back: Divide participants into 2 to 4 groups that move to a new station at a set time (for example every 15 minutes). Each station needs a table and chairs; video stations are best in a separate space; photographs can be printed and laminated.
If space or logistics are difficult: show each station's slides, photographs and videos on one screen to everyone, and keep the time.

read.text:
Facilitation

  • Keep the room silent: participants see the same exercises and must not share answers.
  • Keep the time, and announce warnings.
  • Answer clarifying questions without leading to the answer.
  • Collect the sheets after each station and start marking; enter the marks in the tracking sheet.

steps.title: Station 1: Photographs (15 minutes)
steps.text: 15 photographs on 8 slides, about 90 seconds a slide. Photographs 1 to 10: name the clinical sign and the likely classification. Photographs 11 to 15: breastfeeding: is the attachment good or poor? Make sure everyone can see the signs clearly.

steps.title: Station 2: Video (about 15 minutes)
steps.text: Three video exercises: do these 7 children have chest indrawing? Do these 6 children have sunken eyes? How quickly does each of 5 skin pinches go back? Stop each video before its answers.

steps.title: Station 3: Zinet, a sick child (15 minutes, optional)
steps.text: Read the case, assess and classify with the chart booklet and form, and list the priority treatments. Give a 3-minute warning.

steps.title: Station 4: Mitu, a sick young infant (15 minutes, optional)
steps.text: Read the case, classify, and say what to do immediately.

read.text: Answer keys for all four stations are in the Annexes (Skills stations: answer key).
read.label: Facilitator tip

sections.title: Section 6: Written examination
sections.goal: Give the 30-minute multiple-choice examination in good conditions and mark it quickly.

read.text: Time: 45 minutes. The second part of the assessment: 30 minutes, with 15 minutes spare if the whole group needs more time. Silence and enough space between participants.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
• Participants mark all answers on one answer sheet, not on the question paper, so the papers can be reused.
  • At least two facilitators mark and enter the marks. Punch out the correct answers on a key and lay it over each sheet.
  • The examination, answer sheet and key are in the Annexes, with extra questions for Modules 7, 8 and 9.

steps.title: Time
steps.text: You have 30 minutes. Keep the clock visible to all.

steps.title: Silence
steps.text: Respect silence. If you have a question for the facilitator, do not disturb others.

steps.title: Answers
steps.text: Read the instructions carefully. Mark your answers on the answer sheet, not on the question paper. You may use your chart booklet and recording form.

steps.title: Questions
steps.text: Any questions before we begin?

read.text: Announce 10-minute and 5-minute warnings. Answer clarifying questions without leading. As soon as sheets come in, all facilitators mark, so all are done by the closing.
read.label: Facilitator tip

read.text: The examination is also in this guide as an online exercise (Annexes, Written examination). It starts as a draft: only course authors see it until it is published in the exercise manager.
read.label: In this app

sections.title: Section 7: Next steps and formal closing
sections.goal: Return to the course objectives, guide individual action plans, give the certificates and close the course.

read.text: Time: 45 minutes. Review the course goals and discuss next steps. Participants may write individual action plans. The course evaluation, then certificates. Facilitators not leading this section keep marking the examinations.
read.label: Facilitator summary

read.text:
Materials

  • Slides
  • Flipchart
  • Certificates of completion
  • Individual action plan forms and the course evaluation (Annexes)
7.1 The course objectives

• How have we met these objectives?
  • How will we keep moving forward with them? Discuss further training and other IMNCI learning opportunities.
7.2 Individual action plans (optional)
Introduce the plan, give out the form, and allow 10 minutes. Then ask who will share ideas, and note them on the flipchart:

• ✔ Using IMNCI every day, with every sick child and young infant
  • ✔ Learning more about IMNCI and child health: what further training?
  • ✔ Working with mentors when there are questions
  • ✔ Sharing IMNCI with colleagues and the in-charge
7.3 Certificates
Call each participant forward and recognize one thing about them: a trait, a skill, or something they have shown. Invite each to say a few words about their learning.
7.4 to 7.6 Reflections, evaluation and close

1. Group reflections: what thoughts does each of you have for the group before we close?
  2. Give out the course evaluation and allow about 15 minutes. Honest, detailed feedback is the only way to improve the course; facilitators and the IMNCI programme will review it.
  3. Offer your closing thoughts, thank participants for their time and energy, and close the course.
After the course, follow up participants in their facilities to see how they use IMNCI, and support them.

read.text: Studied in self-study period 1. It teaches the first step for every sick child: greeting the caregiver, checking the general danger signs, and urgent referral.
read.label: This module
Open Module 1
read.text: General danger signs for the sick child
What to check in the learner's work

• ✔ Every recording form has the child's name, age, weight, temperature, problems and initial or follow-up visit
  • ✔ The general danger signs are asked and looked for, one at a time, on every form
  • ✔ A child with any general danger sign is classified ("General danger sign present") and referred urgently after pre-referral treatment
  • ✔ The learner can say the four steps of urgent referral, and what to do when referral is not possible
Signs to see in the clinic
Ask participants to tick these on their checklist of clinical signs. Arrange a demonstration, a video or a mentor for any they have not seen.

• A child who is lethargic or unconscious
  • A child with convulsions in this illness, or convulsing now
  • A child not able to drink or breastfeed
  • A child who vomits everything
Where learners often struggle
A child vomits three times today but keeps some drinks down. Is that a general danger sign?
read.answer: No. "Vomits everything" means nothing stays down: no food, fluid or medicine. Offer a drink and watch if unsure.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: A child is sleepy at the visit. Lethargic?
read.answer: Not necessarily. A lethargic child is drowsy when they should be awake and does not show interest or look at the mother; try to waken the child by talking, clapping or a gentle shake.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: A child has a general danger sign. Should the assessment stop?
read.answer: No: quickly complete the assessment, give the pre-referral treatments, and refer without delay.
read.label: Clarify

sections.title: Module 2: The sick young infant

read.text: Studied in self-study period 1. The longest module of period 1: very severe disease and local infection, jaundice, diarrhoea, treatment, feeding and counselling. Many participants struggle to finish it: set weekly reading goals.
read.label: This module
Open Module 2
read.text: The sick young infant
What to check in the learner's work

• ✔ The young infant form is used for infants up to 2 months, not the sick child form
  • ✔ Breaths are counted twice when the first count is 60 or more
  • ✔ Fever (37.5 °C or above) and low temperature (below 35.5 °C) are measured and recorded
  • ✔ Jaundice is classified by when it appeared, the palms and soles, and the infant's age and weight
  • ✔ Breastfeeding is observed for attachment (four signs) and effective sucking when there is no reason to refer
  • ✔ Weight-for-age is read on the chart for the infant's sex
Signs to see in the clinic
Ask participants to tick these on their checklist of clinical signs. Arrange a demonstration, a video or a mentor for any they have not seen.

• Fast breathing and severe chest indrawing in a young infant
  • Movement only when stimulated
  • Jaundice, including yellow palms and soles
  • A red or draining umbilicus, skin pustules
  • Oral thrush
  • Good and poor attachment at the breast
  • Low weight for age
Where learners often struggle
A young infant has mild chest indrawing. Is it a sign?
read.answer: No. Mild chest indrawing is normal in young infants, whose chest wall is soft. Only severe chest indrawing (very deep and easy to see) is a sign.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Yellow palms and soles in a 10-day-old. How do you classify?
read.answer: SEVERE JAUNDICE: refer urgently. So is any jaundice under 24 hours of age, and in the Sudan booklet any jaundice in an infant under 2.5 kg.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What are the four signs of good attachment?
read.answer: Chin touching the breast; mouth wide open; lower lip turned outward; more areola visible above than below the mouth.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: What are the pre-referral doses for a 3 kg infant?
read.answer: Read them from the chart booklet: the national booklet uses ampicillin 250 mg in 2.1 ml water (1.5 ml for 2.5 to 3.49 kg) and gentamicin. They differ from the WHO module's formulations.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Studied in self-study period 2. Assessing and classifying cough or difficult breathing, amoxicillin for pneumonia, inhalers for wheezing, counselling and follow-up.
read.label: This module
Open Module 3
read.text: Cough or difficult breathing
What to check in the learner's work

• ✔ Breaths are counted for a full minute in a calm child, and fast breathing is judged by age
  • ✔ Chest indrawing, stridor in a calm child, and wheezing are looked for
  • ✔ A child with wheezing and fast breathing or chest indrawing gets a trial of a rapid-acting bronchodilator before classifying
  • ✔ PNEUMONIA is treated with oral amoxicillin for 5 days and followed up in 3 days
  • ✔ A cough of more than 2 weeks or recurrent wheezing is referred for assessment (TB or asthma)
Signs to see in the clinic
Ask participants to tick these on their checklist of clinical signs. Arrange a demonstration, a video or a mentor for any they have not seen.

• Fast breathing
  • Chest indrawing
  • Stridor in a calm child
  • Wheezing
Where learners often struggle
What is fast breathing?
read.answer: 2 months up to 12 months: 50 breaths per minute or more. 12 months up to 5 years: 40 or more.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: A child has chest indrawing but no danger sign or stridor. How do you classify?
read.answer: PNEUMONIA (yellow): oral amoxicillin for 5 days. Chest indrawing alone is no longer a severe classification.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: When do you count the breaths?
read.answer: When the child is calm, before anything that may upset the child. A crying or feeding child breathes faster.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Studied in self-study period 2. Dehydration, persistent diarrhoea and dysentery; Plans A, B and C; ORS and zinc; counselling the four rules of home treatment.
read.label: This module
Open Module 4
read.text: Diarrhoea
What to check in the learner's work

• ✔ Dehydration is classified from two or more signs: general condition, sunken eyes, drinking, skin pinch
  • ✔ The skin pinch is done correctly: lengthwise, all layers, held one second
  • ✔ Every child with diarrhoea receives zinc for 14 days
  • ✔ Plan B is given in the clinic for 4 hours, then the child is reassessed
  • ✔ DYSENTERY is treated with ciprofloxacin for 3 days and followed up in 3 days
  • ✔ The four rules of home treatment are counselled: extra fluid, zinc, continue feeding, when to return
Signs to see in the clinic
Ask participants to tick these on their checklist of clinical signs. Arrange a demonstration, a video or a mentor for any they have not seen.

• Sunken eyes
  • A slow and a very slow skin pinch
  • Restless and irritable
  • Drinking eagerly, thirsty
  • Blood in the stool
Where learners often struggle
A child is restless and irritable but has no other sign. Some dehydration?
read.answer: No: SOME DEHYDRATION needs two signs. With one sign, NO DEHYDRATION.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: Diarrhoea for 14 days with some dehydration. How do you classify?
read.answer: SEVERE PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA: treat the dehydration first, then refer, unless there is another severe classification.
read.label: Clarify

read.text: How long is zinc given?
read.answer: 14 days, even after the diarrhoea has stopped.
read.label: Clarify

sections.title: Planning and managing study groups
sections.goal: Help participants form small, well-run study groups that meet regularly and practise together.

read.text: Working with others matters in distance learning. Group study improves learning (participants test their knowledge by explaining it, discuss problems, and feel responsible to the group) and builds skills: teamwork, analysis, collaboration, organization, and clinical skills when the group practises together.

steps.title: 1. Who is in the group
steps.text: Two to four members; never more than five. Group by where participants live, their clinical setting, and access to the videos (pair those without access with those who have it).

steps.title: 2. Roles
steps.text: Divide tasks: a leader, a scheduler, a note-taker.

steps.title: 3. Procedures
steps.text: Clear guidelines that all members follow; each activity has a clear purpose.

steps.title: 4. Schedule
steps.text: Consider travel time and cost, work commitments, family responsibilities and any disability. Agree the date, time, place, length, what to prepare, and what will be covered.

read.text:
Date and timePlaceMaterialLeader
Week 1, 17:00Health centreModule 1: general danger signsMember A
Week 2, 17:00Health centreModule 2: lessons 1 to 13Member B

Schedule some meetings where there are enough patients to see together: practising in the clinic as a group is strongly recommended.
read.label: Facilitator tip

sections.title: Planning clinical practice sessions
sections.goal: Prepare the clinical site, choose cases, and run each session: demonstrate, practise, give feedback, summarize.

read.text: Clinical practice is where participants learn to perform. They read about a skill, see it demonstrated, apply it in exercises, and most importantly practise it with sick children. It happens in two places: at the face-to-face meetings, and during self-study.
Practice at the meetings
Each meeting has a 60 to 90 minute session around midday. It is a critical chance to mentor skills, so share what you observe with participants immediately.

cards.back: When the site is chosen, explain the sessions to the hospital director and ask permission, from everyone responsible for each ward to be used.
At the facilitators' planning meeting one or two days before, review and practise the clinical skills to be demonstrated.

Note the patient load and peak hours; the patient flow; IMNCI-trained staff who can help; the space for demonstration and practice. Confirm arrangements with the in-charge and ward staff; brief the staff; check medicines and supplies; agree a staff member as session administrator.

read.text:
Supplies

  • Sick child and young infant recording forms
  • Thermometers
  • Scales for children and infants
  • Cups, spoons and clean water to offer fluid
  • Medicines in the most common formulation on the chart

The session administrator

  • Finds suitable children and young infants as they arrive
  • Arranges for them to leave the queue to be seen by participants, and to return to the right station for treatment
  • Makes sure every child seen receives the treatment needed, and agrees who dispenses and gives first doses
  • Checks that clinic staff have been briefed

steps.title: Demonstrate
steps.text: Start with a demonstration, preferably to the whole group: infrequently seen signs, or the new skills of the day.

steps.title: Practise
steps.text: At least one patient for each participant (or pairs or small groups); 20 to 30 minutes for the process, plus discussion. Let more participants see a child with severe or hard signs.

steps.title: Monitor and give feedback
steps.text: Go round and observe, with special attention to the day's new skills and correct use of the chart booklet and form. Work with anyone who struggles until they can do the skill with confidence.

steps.title: Summarize
steps.text: Praise what was done well, especially new or difficult steps, and give suggestions to improve.

read.text:
• One or two facilitators for every 2 to 6 participants (course facilitators and IMNCI-trained staff of the facility).
  • Keep time; have transport ready; participants bring chart booklets and recording forms.
  • Choose children with a variety of signs and classifications, ideally one per participant, and some with infrequent signs: check the participants' checklists of signs first. Ask the caregiver's permission.
Skills focus at each meeting

MeetingFocusFind on the day
1. OrientationThe IMNCI process; general danger signs; the form and charts; demonstration of a young infantChildren with general danger signs; sick young infants
2. Review and practiceGeneral danger signs; the sick young infant; cough or difficult breathing; diarrhoea and dehydrationAs above, plus cough, diarrhoea and dehydration, and signs participants have rarely seen
3. Final synthesisThe whole process and all main symptomsAlso fever, malnutrition and anaemia, ear problems, and children for HIV assessment or well child care

Skin pinch: thumb and first finger; the fold lengthwise along the body; all layers of skin and the tissue beneath; hold one second, release, and watch: very slowly (more than 2 seconds), slowly, or immediately. If a child with some or severe dehydration is seen, gather everyone to see the signs. Participants do not yet treat diarrhoea at Meeting 2: return the child with a note to the clinic staff, or watch the treatment at the ORT corner.

read.text: Practice during self-study
Self-study is where most skills are gained: in the participant's own clinic, with the study group, and with mentors.

• ✔ Keep the modules, chart booklet and recording forms in the clinic, and use them with every case
  • ✔ Practise at the pace of reading: about one week per module. Do not cram.
  • ✔ Fill in recording forms throughout the period, not at the last minute
  • ✔ Set a target number of cases each clinic day
  • ✔ Ask colleagues to call you for cases you rarely see (sick young infants, severe signs)
  • ✔ Ask mentors to observe you and give feedback
  • ✔ Hold some study group meetings where you can practise together

For self-study practice, explain what is expected, check whether each participant's clinic gives enough practice (and arrange more if not), tell them when you are available, and mentor on site or through their mentor.

exercises.title: Distance learning course: final written examination
exercises.source: WHO IMCI distance learning course, facilitator guide (2014), Annex 4.5
narrative: The 30-question written examination of the Final synthesis meeting. You may use your chart booklet and recording form. You have 30 minutes.

questions.question: Which of the following is a major killer of children?
Where in the health system are the IMNCI guidelines designed to be used?
options: In the inpatient ward of a hospital

questions.question: The IMNCI clinical guidelines describe how to manage:
options: Common childhood illnesses that cause high morbidity and mortality

questions.question: The IMNCI clinical guidelines are designed for which age group?
questions.explain: The young infant (up to 2 months) and the child (2 months up to 5 years).

questions.question: Which of the following is a general danger sign?
options: The child is restless or nervous
The child is lethargic or unconscious

questions.question: Which is a main symptom for which every sick child is checked?
What is the cut-off for fast breathing in a child of 10 months?
To classify dehydration in a child with diarrhoea, you LOOK and FEEL for:
Besides dehydration, the mothers of ALL children with diarrhoea are asked:
options: What did the child eat before the diarrhoea started?
Do other family members have diarrhoea?
For how long has the child had diarrhoea?

questions.question: A child is assessed for the main symptom FEVER if the child:
Which children are checked for malnutrition and anaemia?
options: All children with a feeding problem
All children brought to the clinic

questions.question: Pemba is 18 months old, weighs 9 kg, temperature 37 °C, cough for 3 days. He can drink, has not vomited, has had no convulsions, is not lethargic. 45 breaths per minute; no chest indrawing; no stridor. How do you classify him?
options: GENERAL DANGER SIGN and SEVERE PNEUMONIA
questions.explain: 45 is fast breathing from 12 months (40 or more).

questions.question: Heera, 3 years, 10 kg, has diarrhoea for more than 2 weeks with blood in the stool, and no danger sign. She is irritable; eyes not sunken; she drinks but is not thirsty; the skin pinch goes back slowly. How do you classify her?
options: SEVERE PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA, DYSENTERY, SOME DEHYDRATION
questions.explain: Irritable and slow skin pinch: SOME DEHYDRATION. Diarrhoea 14 days or more with dehydration: SEVERE PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA. Blood: DYSENTERY.

questions.question: Anders, 3 years, 37.5 °C, feels hot for 5 days, cough for 3 days, no danger sign. 51 breaths per minute, no chest indrawing or stridor. No stiff neck; runny nose and generalized rash; no clouding of the cornea, pus from the eye or mouth ulcers. How do you classify him (besides the malaria test result)?
Zach, a boy, is 99 cm tall and weighs 12.5 kg. Based on his z-score, how do you classify him?
questions.explain: His weight-for-height is between -3 and -2 z.

questions.question: A child classified SOME DEHYDRATION needs:
options: 4 hours of rehydration with ORS at the clinic (Plan B)
Fluids by IV at the clinic
RUTF and ORS for home treatment

questions.question: Kalisa, 11 months, 8 kg, dry cough for a month, no danger sign. 45 breaths per minute, no chest indrawing or stridor. No diarrhoea, fever or ear problem. No oedema; very pale palms, almost white; MUAC 122 mm. How do you classify him?
options: PNEUMONIA, SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION, SEVERE ANAEMIA
COUGH OR COLD, MODERATE ACUTE MALNUTRITION, SEVERE ANAEMIA
questions.explain: Under 12 months, fast breathing is 50 or more. MUAC 115 up to 125 mm: moderate. Severe pallor: SEVERE ANAEMIA. A cough for more than 2 weeks is also referred for assessment.

questions.question: Sara, 11 months, no danger sign, is classified PNEUMONIA, ACUTE EAR INFECTION, MODERATE ACUTE MALNUTRITION, NO ANAEMIA. She needs urgent referral today.
David, 7 months, no danger sign, is classified MASTOIDITIS, MALARIA, NO ACUTE MALNUTRITION, NO ANAEMIA. He needs urgent referral today.
Isoke, 2 years, no danger sign, is classified diarrhoea with SEVERE DEHYDRATION and SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION. Your clinic can give IV fluids. She needs urgent referral today.
questions.explain: A child with severe acute malnutrition and SEVERE DEHYDRATION is referred urgently (Module 6). The 2014 key gave FALSE.

questions.question: Ahmed comes for follow-up of PNEUMONIA. He had fast breathing and has been taking amoxicillin. His mother says he is still sick and vomited twice today. Which sign will you look for when you reassess him?
options: Whether he is restless or irritable
questions.explain: At the pneumonia follow-up, check for general danger signs and assess cough: chest indrawing, stridor, breathing rate.

questions.question: Oko, 2 years, is classified VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE, CHRONIC EAR INFECTION and ANAEMIA, and needs referral. Which of his treatments is an urgent pre-referral treatment?
options: Treat the child to prevent low blood sugar
Assess feeding and counsel the mother on feeding

questions.question: A 6-month-old (7.4 kg) has PNEUMONIA and MASTOIDITIS and can drink. What do you give at the clinic now?
options: The first dose of oral amoxicillin, 5 ml of syrup 250 mg/5 ml, and paracetamol, then refer urgently
Cotrimoxazole syrup 5 ml, and treat at home
Amoxicillin for 5 days, and follow up in 3 days
questions.explain: MASTOIDITIS needs urgent referral after the first dose of antibiotic. In the national booklet this is oral amoxicillin if the child can take oral medicine. The 2014 examination asked about cotrimoxazole and ceftriaxone, which are no longer first line here.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the four rules of home treatment for diarrhoea?
options: Stop breastfeeding until the diarrhoea stops
questions.explain: The four rules: give extra fluid, give zinc, continue feeding, know when to return. The third option was changed from "maintain feeding", which is also a rule.

questions.question: A child has NO DEHYDRATION, PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA, NO ANAEMIA and no acute malnutrition. Which sign do you teach the mother to return immediately for?
options: The child vomits more than 4 times a day
Not able to drink or breastfeed
Palmar pallor not better in 30 days

questions.question: Rena, 5 months, 4 kg, is classified SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION. She breastfeeds 4 times in 24 hours and has cow's milk by bottle twice a day; nothing else; no change during the illness. What is her feeding problem?
options: She is not breastfed enough: at least 8 times in 24 hours
She should receive more cow's milk

questions.question: What feeding advice does Rena's mother need?
options: Give cow's milk in addition to breastfeeding
If other fluid is given, a bottle is safer than a cup

questions.question: The health worker asks: "What foods will you give the child?" The mother answers: "Nutritious foods." What is a good second checking question?
options: Do you remember what foods are nutritious?
What are these nutritious foods that you can give the child?
Yes, you will give nutritious foods.

questions.question: How could you ask "Do you remember how to give the syrup?" as a good checking question?
options: Do you know what syrup to give?
Will you remember to give the syrup twice a day?
How will you give the syrup?

questions.question: A child returns for follow-up of PNEUMONIA and still has fast breathing. Before deciding on treatment, you find out whether the caregiver gave the oral antibiotic properly.

exercises.title: Distance learning course: examination questions for Modules 7, 8 and 9
exercises.source: WHO IMCI distance learning course, facilitator guide (2014), Annex 4.6
narrative: Extra examination questions for the ear problems, well child and HIV/AIDS modules.

questions.question: Ear problems. Dana, 18 months, 9 kg, no danger sign, no cough, diarrhoea or fever. No ear pain; discharge for 3 or 4 days; pus draining from the right ear; no tender swelling behind the ears. How do you classify her?
Ear problems. To be classified MASTOIDITIS, a child must have:
options: Severe ear pain and redness behind the ear

questions.question: Well child. What is the interval between doses of pneumococcal vaccine?
Well child. At what age does vitamin A start?
Well child. What play would you recommend for a child of 6 to 9 months?
options: Stacking objects and putting them inside each other
Naming simple words, such as household objects

questions.question: Well child. A child beginning to crawl is an example of what kind of skill?
Well child. What do you recommend about chemicals and medicines at home?
options: Store them in clear water or soda bottles so they are easy to identify
Store them in child-resistant containers out of reach
Tell children to stay out of their parents' things

questions.question: HIV. What is the role of the immune system?
options: Ridding the body of toxins in urine

questions.question: HIV. What does a CD4 count or percentage tell you?
options: The amount of HIV in the body
How much HIV has been destroyed by cotrimoxazole
How severely HIV has damaged the immune system

questions.question: HIV. Which is an opportunistic infection?
HIV. A child can be infected with HIV by the mother:
options: At delivery, and after birth by kissing
During pregnancy, at delivery, and after birth by hugging or holding
During pregnancy, at delivery, and after birth through breastfeeding

questions.question: HIV. Mother-to-child transmission is reduced by:
options: Antiretroviral drugs that lower the mother's viral load in pregnancy, delivery and breastfeeding

questions.question: HIV. Tsidi is 13 months old; her mother is HIV-positive. She has never been tested and has not breastfed for 7 months. Which test?
questions.explain: Under 18 months, a positive antibody test shows only exposure; a virological test confirms or excludes infection.

questions.question: HIV. What is a virological (PCR) test?
options: A test for antibodies, recommended for all children under 18 months
A test recommended for all children who are breastfeeding
A test for the virus itself, recommended for children under 18 months

questions.question: HIV. Zinsi, 8 months, breastfeeding, mother HIV-positive, PCR negative, no features of HIV.
options: Assume she is free of HIV
Repeat the PCR 6 weeks after breastfeeding stops
Repeat the PCR after 18 months of age

questions.question: HIV. Leboheng, 3 months; his mother is HIV-positive; he has not been tested. How do you classify him?
HIV. An 8-week-old boy abandoned at birth had a negative PCR at 6 weeks. How do you classify him?
HIV. Greg, 20 months, has a positive antibody test and is classified CONFIRMED HIV INFECTION. What is important now?
options: Give nevirapine prophylaxis once a day

questions.question: HIV. Which is a severe sign in a child on ART?
questions.explain: Severe abdominal pain (with difficult breathing), yellow eyes and severe skin rash mean stop and refer urgently. The 2014 key gives "nausea", which is a mild side effect.

questions.question: HIV. What do you tell the caregiver about ART?
options: It can be taken any time of day
It must be taken every day, for life, at the same times
Double the dose after a missed day

questions.question: HIV. Liam, 7 months, had a negative PCR at 6 months and stopped breastfeeding at 3 months. Should he start cotrimoxazole?
questions.explain: His negative test came more than 6 weeks after breastfeeding stopped, so HIV is excluded and cotrimoxazole is not needed (Module 8). The 2014 key gave "yes".

questions.question: HIV. Jo started first-line ART 6 weeks ago and now has yellow eyes. What do you do?
options: Stop the medicines and refer urgently

questions.question: HIV. Starting ART in a child with confirmed infection follows six steps.
questions.explain: There are five steps: confirm infection, make sure the caregiver can give ART, decide whether ART can start at this level, record the baseline, start ART and cotrimoxazole.

questions.question: HIV. Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis has reduced deaths among HIV-infected children.
HIV. With good adherence, ART cures HIV.
HIV. You may delay starting ART if the caregiver is not ready to give it every day.
HIV. A child on ART who responds well does not need regular follow-up.
